newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ fires minister to ease coalition tensions.
newsitem.headline: NZ fires minister to ease coalition tensions.

text.p: New Zealand's two-party coalition government moved to defuse growing internal tensions by sacking a junior health minister on Thursday.
The move left the key portfolio entirely in the hands of the dominant conservative National Party and took an inexperienced member of junior partner New Zealand First out of the executive.
The sacked minister, Neil Kirton, said he would consider his future options and did not rule out resigning from parliament.
Deputy Prime Minister and NZ First leader Winston Peters said he had fired Kirton as Associate Health Minister "in the interest of good government" for speaking out of turn.
"The reality is we have to make a government work in a difficult time," he told national radio news.
Peters told reporters the move followed a long-running series of disciplinary problems with Kirton and members of his staff, who had defied specific party orders.
The latest order defied by Kirton was a ban issued on Wednesday on talking to the media. Peters said the order "came directly from me and this is not the first time I've said it".

"Last night I made it very clear to Mr Kirton that there was to be no media comment pending a meeting between the Prime Minister and myself to sort out the public dispute between the two health ministers," Peters said in a statement.
"This morning Mr Kirton went on radio in disregard to that clear instruction and accordingly I have dismissed him," he said.

While he regretted the move he said it had become necessary, as a public dispute between the associate minister and senior Health Minister Bill English over health policy risked becoming "a major crisis".
Kirton was the latest NZ First member to draw flak from its political opponents and from within the coalition.
Political observers said Kirton's apparent difficulty in avoiding conflicts of interest and holding to the government line stemmed partly from inexperience, a common problem among NZ First MPs.
The nationalist party shot to the political forefront late last year after winning the balance of power in the country's first elections under a type of proportional representation.
Earlier this year Peters was caught in the crossfire of a series of minor scandals, mainly involving Maori MP Tukoroirangi Morgan, culminating in a fraud squad report that exonerated him.
At the same time the party's popularity has slumped from near 13 percent at last October's general election. An opinion poll for July showed its support at 3.8 percent.
Peters admitted on Thursday that the move to oust Kirton might leave the coalition's voting power depleted in parliament if the MP chose to leave the party.
In the 120-seat single chamber parliament National has 44 and NZ First 17 seats, giving them a narrow voting majority.
According to the rules, if Kirton were to resign his seat he would be replaced by the next person on the NZ First party list, leaving the overall balance of power unchanged.
However, another option is that Kirton might resign the party whip, which would give him an independent status in parliament that is still unclear under the proportional rules.
